Living Organisms: Characteristics, Adaptations and Classification

MYP 5 / Grade 10 Biology • Independent study pack • about three lessons • Prepared by Mr George Apidi
How do living organisms survive in their environment, and how do scientists sort and name the millions of different kinds?
Type your name and class first. Work in order. Press Save step at the end of each step: it marks your answers, gives you feedback and sends your work to your teacher. Your work is kept on this device if you close the page.

By the end of this pack you can

  • describe the seven characteristics of living organisms (MRS GREN);
  • define adaptation, tell STRUCTURAL from BEHAVIOURAL adaptations, and analyse adaptations shown in a video;
  • list the five kingdoms and the five vertebrate classes, with the features of each;
  • list the eight taxonomic ranks, define a species and write scientific names correctly;
  • describe why we classify, and use and build dichotomous keys.

STEP 1 · QUESTION

The wildebeest and the stick insect

about 10 min
  • Every July, more than a million wildebeest cross the Mara River from Tanzania into Kenya's Maasai Mara, risking crocodiles on the way (Figure A).
  • In a forest nearby, a stick insect sits so still and looks so like a twig that a bird flies straight past it (Figure B).
  • Both are alive, both survive in their own way, and both have a scientific name that scientists in every country understand.

STEP 2 · EXPLORE

Characteristics of life and adaptations

about 40 min

Your choice: how will you learn Part A?

▶ Oak National Academy: The common processes of all living organisms

Part A · The characteristics of living organisms

Notes

  • All living organisms carry out seven processes: MRS GREN. An organism does each one at some stage of its life.
  • Movement: an action that changes the position of the organism or part of it (plants move too, slowly).
  • Respiration: chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy.
  • Sensitivity: detecting changes in the environment (stimuli) and responding to them.
  • Growth: a permanent increase in size and dry mass.
  • Reproduction: processes that make more of the same kind of organism.
  • Excretion: removal of the waste products of metabolism, e.g. carbon dioxide and urea. Removing undigested food (egestion) is NOT excretion.
  • Nutrition: taking in materials for energy, growth and development.

(a) List the seven characteristics of living organisms. 2 marks

Part B · Adaptations: how organisms survive

Notes: what is an adaptation?

  • An ADAPTATION is an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment.
  • STRUCTURAL adaptations are features of the BODY: shape, colour, covering or parts.
  • BEHAVIOURAL adaptations are things the organism DOES: the way it acts.
  • (Extension) Functional adaptations are processes inside the body, e.g. desert animals making very concentrated urine.
STRUCTURAL adaptations: features of the body
OrganismAdaptationHow it helps survival
Leopard (Fig. 2)Spotted coat that matches dry grass and shadows: CAMOUFLAGE.Creeps close to prey without being seen.
Stick insect (Fig. B)Long thin brown body and legs shaped like a twig.Predators such as birds do not notice it.
Cactus (Fig. 3)Leaves reduced to SPINES; thick, swollen, waxy green stem.Less surface area so less water lost by transpiration; spines stop animals eating it; stem stores water and photosynthesises.
Camel (Fig. 4)Wide flat feet; long eyelashes; hump of fat.Feet do not sink in sand; eyelashes keep out sand; fat is an energy store.
Jackson's chameleon (Fig. 5)Green skin; eyes that move separately; long sticky tongue; gripping feet.Hidden among leaves; spots insects all around; catches them at a distance.
BEHAVIOURAL adaptations: things the organism does
BehaviourWhat happensHow it helps survival
Bird MIGRATION (Fig. 6)White storks fly about 10 000 km from Europe to East and southern Africa each autumn.Winter in Europe means little food; Africa has food all year.
Wildebeest migration (Fig. A)Herds move between the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara following the rains.They follow fresh grass and water; calving at the same time protects the young.
HIBERNATION (Figs 7, 8)Bears and dormice sleep deeply through winter; heart rate, breathing and body temperature drop.Saves energy when food is scarce; they live on stored fat.
Weaver bird nests (Fig. 9)Nests woven and hung from the tips of thin branches, often over water.Snakes and monkeys cannot reach the eggs and chicks.
Other local examplesLions hunt at night; elephants spray mud and flap their ears.Cooler hunting; mud protects skin from sun; flapping ears lose heat.

STEP 3 · TEST

The five kingdoms and the vertebrate classes

about 30 min
▶ Optional video: Classification into kingdoms and domains

Notes: classification starts with the cell

  • CLASSIFICATION is the grouping and naming of organisms based on their shared characteristics.
  • Organisms are first sorted by cell type. Prokaryotes have no nucleus. Eukaryotes have a nucleus.
  • Eukaryotes form FOUR kingdoms: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protoctista. Prokaryotes form the fifth: Monera (bacteria).
  • All five kingdoms carry out MRS GREN, but differ in cell structure, body organisation and nutrition.
KingdomCellsBodyNutrition and other featuresExamples
MONERA (prokaryotes)NO nucleus; DNA as a loop; cell wall (not cellulose); no mitochondriaunicellularMost feed on other organisms (decomposers, parasites); some photosynthesise. Binary fission.E. coli, Lactobacillus in yoghurt
PROTOCTISTANucleus; some have chloroplastsmostly unicellularSome feed like animals (Amoeba); some photosynthesise like plants (Euglena). Water or moist places.Amoeba, Euglena, Plasmodium (malaria)
FUNGINucleus; cell wall of CHITIN; no chlorophyllthread-like HYPHAE forming a mycelium (yeast is unicellular)SAPROTROPHIC: release enzymes onto food and absorb the products. Reproduce by SPORES. Store glycogen.Rhizopus, mushrooms, yeast
PLANTAENucleus; CELLULOSE cell wall; chloroplasts; large vacuolemulticellularMake their own food by PHOTOSYNTHESIS. Store starch or sucrose.maize, ferns, acacia
ANIMALIANucleus; NO cell wall; no chloroplastsmulticellularFeed on organic substances made by other organisms. Most move the whole body; nervous system. Store glycogen.lion, elephant, insects, humans

Part B · The five classes of vertebrates

  • Animals with a backbone are VERTEBRATES. They are sorted into five classes by body covering, breathing, reproduction and body temperature.
  • Endothermic animals keep a constant body temperature. Ectothermic animals' temperature changes with their surroundings.
ClassBody coveringBreathingReproductionTemperatureOther featuresExample
MAMMALSfur or hairlungsmostly live young; feed young on MILK from mammary glandsendothermicexternal ears (pinna); different types of teethAfrican elephant
BIRDSFEATHERSlungshard-shelled eggsendothermicbeak, no teeth; forelimbs are wingsAfrican fish eagle
REPTILESdry, scaly skinlungsleathery-shelled eggs laid on landectothermicNile crocodile
AMPHIBIANSmoist, smooth skin, no scalesgills as larvae; lungs and skin as adultsjelly-covered eggs laid in waterectothermiclive on land and in waterfrog
FISHwet scalesgillsjelly-covered eggs laid in waterectothermicfins; lateral lineNile tilapia

STEP 4 · EXPLAIN

Ranks, species, binomial names and why we classify

about 30 min

From the history books

  • In 1735 the Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus published Systema Naturae. He sorted organisms into groups inside groups and gave every species a two-part Latin name. Scientists still use his system today.
▶ Optional video: Classification and species

Notes: the hierarchy of classification

  • EIGHT main ranks, largest to smallest: DOMAIN → KINGDOM → PHYLUM → CLASS → ORDER → FAMILY → GENUS → SPECIES (Figure 20).
  • Memory aid: “Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.”
  • A kingdom holds many organisms that share only a few features; a species holds organisms that share almost all their features.
  • The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
RankLionPolar bearHuman
DomainEukaryaEukaryaEukarya
KingdomAnimaliaAnimaliaAnimalia
PhylumChordataChordataChordata
ClassMammaliaMammaliaMammalia
OrderCarnivoraCarnivoraPrimates
FamilyFelidaeUrsidaeHominidae
GenusPantheraUrsusHomo
Speciesleomaritimussapiens
Scientific namePanthera leoUrsus maritimusHomo sapiens

Notes: what is a species?

  • A SPECIES is a group of organisms that can reproduce with one another to produce FERTILE offspring.
  • A horse (Equus caballus) and a donkey (Equus asinus) can mate, but their offspring, the mule, is infertile. So they are DIFFERENT species in the SAME genus.

Notes: binomial nomenclature

  • A TWO-NAME system: GENUS then SPECIES. Each name is unique and Latin (or made to look Latin).
  • Only the GENUS has a capital letter: Homo sapiens, Panthera leo.
  • Typed: italics. Handwritten: underline each word separately: Panthera leo.
  • After the first use the genus may be shortened: P. leo.

Notes: why do scientists classify organisms?

  • A common international language. “Simba”, “lion”, “león”, but Panthera leo to every scientist.
  • Placing new species. A new organism's features are compared with known ones so it can be placed in the right genus, family and so on.
  • Tracing evolution. Organisms in the same group usually share a common ancestor (Figure 19).
  • Studying and protecting biodiversity. You cannot conserve a species you cannot identify.

STEP 5 · CHALLENGE

Use a dichotomous key, then build your own

about 35 min

Notes: dichotomous keys

  • A dichotomous key identifies organisms using a series of PAIRED statements (“dichotomous” = dividing into two).
  • At each step you choose ONE of two statements. Each choice names the organism or tells you which step to go to next.
  • Use features you can SEE or MEASURE: never “big” without a comparison, never behaviour you cannot observe.
  • A key for n organisms has n − 1 pairs of statements.

Build a key

How to construct a dichotomous key

  1. List the organisms. Find ONE feature that splits them into two groups (e.g. has a nucleus / has no nucleus).
  2. Write it as a PAIR of statements, 1a / 1b. Each must be true for one group and false for the other.
  3. Split each group again with a new pair. Keep going until every organism has its own end point.
  4. Number every pair. Each statement ends with an organism's NAME or “go to …”.
  5. TEST it: pick an organism, start at 1, and check you arrive at the right name.

Your choice: how will you build your key? (same marks)
